rationale: SI-4 requires monitoring systems to detect attacks, unauthorized use, and anomalous behavior; Anomaly Detection implements this through behavioral baselines for systems and models and alerting tied to incident playbooks.

CA-7 requires an ongoing monitoring strategy with defined metrics, frequencies and reporting, AU-12 audit record generation and AU-6 audit record review, analysis and reporting; Continuous Monitoring provides that program across digital and AI systems, including model performance and drift.
SI-4 requires monitoring for indicators of compromise and attack; IOC Detection implements this for conventional and AI-native indicators such as adversarial prompts and model abuse.

IR-4 requires an incident handling capability covering preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery; Incident Management provides that capability for security and AI incidents.

SR-3 requires supply chain controls and processes and SR-5 requires acquisition strategies and tools to manage supply chain risk; Monitor Third Parties supplies the ongoing oversight of supplier performance and security posture these controls depend on.

CA-2 requires assessing control effectiveness through a defined assessment plan and producing an assessment report; Performing Security Assessments conducts independent, systematic security testing across digital and AI environments.
CA-8 requires penetration testing of systems and components; Penetration Testing simulates adversarial attacks against systems and models to evaluate resilience.

RA-5 requires vulnerability monitoring and scanning with remediation of findings within defined response times; Vulnerability Testing identifies and drives mitigation of exploitable weaknesses across systems, applications, and AI components.

IR-3 requires testing incident response capability and CP-4 requires testing the contingency plan, both explicitly including tabletop exercises; Tabletop Exercises (BCDR) runs scheduled exercises across cyber, disaster recovery, and AI failure scenarios and updates playbooks from the results.

SA-11 requires developer security testing including static and dynamic analysis, and SI-2 requires identifying and correcting flaws; Code Scanning keeps application and AI codebases free of known defects and insecure configurations.

PM-16 requires a threat awareness program that shares threat information; Threat Intelligence collects and applies threat intelligence, including AI-specific adversarial tactics, to defensive decisions.
CM-3 requires configuration change control with documented review, approval, and testing; Change Management provides that process for system and AI changes.
SA-15 requires a documented development process, standards, and tools that address security and privacy; the Software Development Lifecycle provides that process.
PS-3 requires personnel screening, PS-4 personnel termination, and PS-5 personnel transfer; Human Resources manages hiring, role changes, and departures under those requirements.

PM-19 requires a senior privacy official with authority over the privacy program and PM-1 places that program within organization-wide governance; the Privacy Oversight Committee provides governance and decision authority on privacy and sensitive-data handling.
PM-1 requires the security program plan to define coordination and oversight among organizational entities; the Security Oversight Committee provides that governance body.
PM-6 requires measures of performance for the security program and CA-7 metrics for ongoing monitoring; Performance Metrics defines and reports those measures.
PM-19 requires a privacy program leadership role and PT-1 PII processing policy and procedures; M.PR runs day-to-day privacy operations under them.

SR-2 and SR-3 require a supply chain risk management plan and controls, and SA-4 requires security and privacy requirements in acquisition contracts; Third-Party Risk Management assesses vendors and writes security requirements into their agreements.
RA-3 requires ongoing risk assessment and PM-9 an organization-wide risk strategy; Cybersecurity Risk Management continuously evaluates threats, vulnerabilities, and exposure within that strategy.

PM-15 requires contacts with security groups and associations and PM-31 a continuous monitoring strategy with reporting to officials; Reporting delivers structured, risk-informed reporting to governance bodies. Partial alignment, as PM-15 addresses external rather than internal reporting.
CA-2(1) requires independent assessors or assessment teams; External Audit: Security Audit obtains that independent validation of the security program through certification or attestation.

IR-6 requires personnel to report suspected incidents within a defined period and IR-7 an incident response support resource for users; Reporting Channels provide the accessible, responsive routes to report risks, incidents and concerns.
CA-2 requires control assessments by qualified assessors and CA-7 ongoing assessment; Internal Audit: Security Audit independently assesses control design and operating effectiveness.

CA-2 requires planned, independent control assessments with documented results, and CA-7 requires ongoing assessment within a monitoring program; Internal Audit provides a chartered, independent, risk-based audit plan with tracked findings and corrective actions.

SA-11 requires developer testing and evaluation of controls and CA-2 assessment of implemented controls; Testing plans and executes functional, security, reliability and safety tests before production.
CA-2 requires assessing whether controls are implemented correctly and producing the desired outcome, and CA-7 ongoing assessment; Verification confirms systems meet design and policy requirements.

CM-8 requires an accurate, current system component inventory and PM-5 an organization-wide system inventory; System Asset Management maintains an authoritative CMDB with owners, classification, and interconnections.

AC-19 requires usage restrictions and configuration for mobile devices and AC-20 controls use of external systems including personally owned devices; BYOD Asset Management controls risk from personally owned devices accessing organizational systems.

PM-5 requires a system inventory and CM-8 a component inventory, which data flow mapping depends on; Data Mapping documents where data resides and how it moves. PM-5(1), the inventory of PII, is the closer fit for personal data.
RA-3 requires identifying threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, and impact; Risk Identification identifies risks across cyber, privacy, safety, ethics, and AI for consistent analysis.
PM-12 requires an insider threat program with a cross-discipline incident handling team; Insider Threat establishes that program with HR, Security, and Legal oversight and behavioral monitoring.
SR-2 requires a supply chain risk management plan; Supply Chain Risk identifies and manages risk from software, model, and dataset suppliers under that plan.
CA-7 requires monitoring against defined metrics and thresholds and RA-3 risk determinations against tolerance; Security Thresholds defines the measurable limits that trigger action.

RA-3 requires threat identification in risk assessments, PM-16 a threat awareness program and SI-5 handling of security alerts and advisories; Threat Management continuously identifies, assesses and tracks threats to systems and AI assets.
IR-6 requires reporting incidents to designated authorities within defined time frames; Regulatory Reporting meets those notification obligations to regulators.
IR-6 requires reporting incident information to designated authorities; Law Enforcement Partners maintains the relationships and procedures for reporting to law enforcement.

PM-15 requires contacts with security groups and associations and PM-16 a threat awareness program; Information-Sharing Communities participates in ISACs and similar forums to exchange threat information.

IR-8(1) requires the incident response plan to include breach procedures, including notification of affected individuals, and IR-6 requires reporting to authorities; Privacy Notification Requirements notifies affected individuals and authorities after a verified breach.
IR-6 requires personnel to report suspected incidents and AT-2 awareness training that covers how to report; Personnel ensures staff know and use the internal reporting path.
IR-6 requires incident reporting to designated officials and PM-1 senior management involvement in the security program; Top Management keeps executives informed and engaged during incidents.

IR-4 requires coordinating incident handling activities across the organization and IR-5 tracking and documenting incidents; the Incident Response Team maintains secure coordination channels, war-room roles, and chronological decision logs.

IR-6 requires incident reporting and PM-1 senior-level approval within the security program; Public Updates / Disclosures governs approved external statements about incidents. Partial alignment, as SP 800-53 does not address public disclosure directly.
IR-4 includes recovery in incident handling and CP-10 requires system recovery and reconstitution to a known state; Recovery Activity & Restoration restores services after an incident.
IR-4 requires incident handling that includes containment; Containment isolates affected assets, blocks malicious activity and preserves evidence.
IR-4 requires eradication within incident handling and SI-2 correction of flaws; Eradication removes malicious artifacts, vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that caused the incident.
CP-10 requires recovery and reconstitution and IR-4 recovery within incident handling; Disaster Recovery (RESPOND) restores systems and data from a clean, trusted state post-incident.

CP-2 requires maintaining essential mission and business functions despite disruption and CP-11 alternate communications protocols; Business Continuity (RESPOND) keeps critical operations running during response and recovery.
IR-4 requires incident handling, IR-5 incident monitoring, and IR-6 incident reporting; Incident Response: Cybersecurity provides the end-to-end response capability for cyber incidents.

IR-8(1) requires the incident response plan to address breaches involving PII, including notification and assessment, and IR-6 reporting to designated authorities; Incident Response: Privacy manages personal data breaches to those obligations.

IR-4 requires incorporating lessons learned from incident handling into procedures, training and testing, and IR-8 updating the incident response plan from lessons learned; Incident Lessons Learned turns every incident into measurable control improvement.
PM-1 requires an organization-wide information security program plan approved by a senior official; Top Management Commitment supplies the leadership endorsement and resourcing that plan requires.

PM-1 requires the program plan to define roles, responsibilities, and coordination among organizational entities; Charters & Committees establishes the chartered oversight bodies that carry out that coordination.
PM-1 requires senior-level approval and periodic review of the security program plan; Executive Leadership & Board Oversight provides that senior accountability and strategic direction.
PL-4 requires rules of behavior that users acknowledge before receiving access; COC: Acceptable Use defines permitted and prohibited use of systems, data, and AI tools for personnel.
PM-1 requires an organization-wide program plan supported by policy; Core Policies provides the hierarchical policy architecture spanning security, privacy, and AI.
PL-1 requires planning policy and procedures and PM-1 requires the security program plan; Security Policies sets enforceable security expectations that these documents formalize.
IR-1 and CP-1 require incident response and contingency planning policies and procedures; Response & Resilience Policies provides them, including AI-specific failure modes.

PT-1 requires PII processing and transparency policy and procedures and PM-19 requires a privacy program leadership role; Privacy Policies establishes the rules for fair, lawful processing of personal data.
PS-1 requires personnel security policy and procedures; HR Policies defines the personnel practices that support secure and ethical conduct.

SR-1 requires supply chain risk management policy and procedures and PM-30 requires an organization-wide supply chain risk management strategy; Supply-Chain Policies sets the standards suppliers of software, models, and datasets must meet.

PM-1 anchors data-governance policy in the security program and MP-1 requires media protection policy and procedures; Data-Governance Policies sets rules for data quality, integrity, and handling. Partial alignment, as SP 800-53 does not address data quality.
PL-1 requires planning procedures and CM-6 requires documented configuration settings; Security Standards defines the technical hardening baselines that CM-6 settings implement.
IR-1 and CP-1 require incident response and contingency procedures; Response & Resilience Standards provides the standardized recovery and continuity procedures that implement those policies.
PM-19 requires a senior privacy official to lead a privacy program that ensures compliance with privacy law; Data Privacy Compliance provides that compliance oversight and accountability.

CM-10 requires using software and documentation in accordance with contracts and copyright law and controlling peer-to-peer file sharing; IP Management tracks open-source and third-party licenses and protects proprietary code, models, and data. SP 800-53 covers only the software-licensing part of IP management.

PM-18 requires an organization-wide privacy program plan, PM-19 a privacy program leadership role, and PT-1 PII processing policy; the Privacy Program establishes and maintains the enterprise privacy management program these controls describe.

RA-3 requires risk assessments and PM-9 requires an organization-wide risk management strategy; the Risk Management Framework integrates security, AI, privacy, and operational risk under one enterprise approach.

RA-3 requires risk determinations to be made against organizational risk tolerance; Risk Appetite and Tolerance sets the approved thresholds those determinations rely on. PM-9, which requires risk tolerance in the risk management strategy, would also fit.

RA-3 requires cybersecurity risk assessments and PM-9 an organization-wide risk management strategy; the Cybersecurity Risk-Management Program continuously identifies, analyzes, and treats cyber risk within that strategy.
SR-2 requires a supply chain risk management plan and SR-3 supply chain controls and processes; the Third-Party Risk-Management Program establishes the governance for vendor and supplier risk.

PL-2 requires system security plans that describe authorization boundaries, interconnections, and the operating environment, and PM-5 a system inventory; System Boundaries maintains the boundary diagrams, trust zones, and interface inventories these plans document.

PM-11 requires defining mission and business processes with consideration of security and privacy; Goals & Context translates mission into risk-informed governance goals from internal and external context.
PL-2 requires documented system scope and categorization and PM-5 an organizational system inventory; Security Scope determines which assets are in scope and the protection each warrants.

AT-2 requires security and privacy literacy training and awareness for all users and AT-3 role-based training; Cybersecurity Training delivers the foundational and advanced security awareness those controls require.
AT-3 requires role-based training for personnel with assigned security and privacy roles; Governance Training develops that literacy for leadership, risk owners and committees.
MP-3 requires media marking and MP-4 media storage; Classification & Handling applies classification labels and handling rules to information and media.
SC-13 requires cryptography that meets applicable law and standards; Cryptographic Management governs algorithm selection, key management, and encryption use.
CM-7 requires least functionality and SI-3 malicious code protection; Endpoint Security hardens endpoints and deploys anti-malware and EDR.

IA-2 requires unique identification and authentication of organizational users and IA-4 identifier management; Identity Management governs identity issuance, authentication, and lifecycle for users and service accounts.
SC-7 requires boundary protection and AC-4 information flow enforcement; Network Security segments networks and controls traffic between zones.
PT-1 requires PII processing and transparency policy and procedures; Privacy Controls implements privacy safeguards in systems that process personal data.
SC-3 requires isolating security functions from non-security functions; Platform Security hardens and isolates the platforms that host systems and AI workloads.
PE-2 requires physical access authorizations and PE-3 physical access control at entry points; Access Controls enforces badging, visitor vetting, and secure-area entry.

PE-11 requires emergency power, PE-13 fire protection, PE-14 environmental controls, and PE-15 water damage protection; Environment Controls provides UPS and generators, fire suppression, HVAC with alerting, and water leak detection (P.PY-02-req-01, req-02).

PE-10 requires emergency shutoff capability and PE-12 emergency lighting for exits and evacuation routes; Safety & Security provides coordinated emergency power-off for compute clusters (P.PY-03-req-04) and evacuation procedures (P.PY-03-req-01).

CP-2 requires a contingency plan, CP-7 an alternate processing site, and CP-9 system backup; Resilience Controls engineers recovery objectives, multi-region failover, and immutable backups with restore testing.

CP-2 requires a contingency plan with recovery objectives and roles and CP-2(8) identification of critical assets; Business Continuity maintains BIA-driven continuity strategies, workarounds and communications.

CP-9 requires system backups with integrity protection and CP-10 recovery and reconstitution to a known state; Disaster Recovery restores systems, data and AI pipelines to target RTO/RPO from immutable, tested backups.

SR-4 requires provenance for systems and components, SR-11 component authenticity and SA-9 security requirements for external system services; Supply Chain ensures provenance, integrity and security of third-party components including AI models and APIs.
SA-8 requires security and privacy engineering principles and SA-11 developer testing; Secure Development applies both throughout design and build.
